Chapter 2: Questioning the Stories That Shape Reality.
Once you start noticing just how much inherited beliefs shape the way you see the world, the next step is to get curious. What if you could question the stories you’ve always taken for granted? These aren’t just random thoughts—they’re the narratives that shape how you see yourself, what you think is possible, and even how you define happiness.
Some of these stories are deeply personal. Maybe it’s something like, “I’m not creative.” Others are more collective, like, “Success means you always have to be achieving something new.” The thing is, if you never stop to examine them, these stories can quietly limit what you believe you’re capable of. They can chip away at your sense of joy—without you even realizing it.
So, how do you challenge these narratives? Well, it starts with being willing to step outside your comfort zone. Imagine you’re a fish, swimming in water that you’ve never noticed before. Suddenly, you realize—hey, this water is affecting everything I do. That’s what it’s like to spot these invisible stories. It doesn’t mean you have to toss out every belief you’ve ever had. It just means looking at them honestly, shining a light on them, and seeing if they still make sense.
Here’s a practical way to think about it: treat your beliefs like working hypotheses, not absolute facts. Scientists do this all the time—they test their assumptions, gather evidence, and update their thinking. You can do the same with the stories you tell yourself. Let’s say you believe you’re “bad at relationships.” Instead of accepting that at face value, look back at times when things actually went well. Or maybe ask friends what they appreciate about you. Chances are, you’ll find some cracks in the story.
There are a few steps you can try:
First, identify those core stories—the ones that shape how you see yourself and what you expect from life. Next, ask yourself: are these stories based on your own direct experience, or did you pick them up from someone else? Then, look for exceptions. Can you think of moments that challenge the narrative you’ve always believed? And finally, imagine how things might change if you let go, or even rewrote, that old story.
Remember, this isn’t about tearing yourself down or questioning everything until you’re lost. It’s really about self-compassion and curiosity. Every one of us has stories that once made sense, but maybe aren’t serving us anymore. When you gently loosen your grip on them, you create space for something new to grow.
For example, someone who’s always believed, “people can’t change,” might struggle with forgiveness. But if they start questioning that—maybe by remembering times they or someone else have actually grown—they open up to hope and acceptance. Or, if you feel stuck with the belief that “life is a struggle,” what happens when you start noticing small moments of ease or joy? Suddenly, the narrative doesn’t hold as much power.
Of course, this work can feel uncomfortable. Letting go of familiar stories can feel like losing a part of yourself. There might be uncertainty, or even fear. But honestly? That discomfort is often a sign of growth. It means your old framework is stretching, making room for a more authentic, more expansive version of you.
Over time, getting into the habit of questioning your stories becomes a real source of strength. It helps you bounce back, adapt, and feel more in control of your own life. Instead of being at the mercy of old inherited ideas, you start writing your own story. And that’s really at the heart of personal empowerment and true happiness.
